title: Hours Between Two Times Calculator 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
description: Calculate exact hours & minutes between two times. Handles overnight shifts, AM/PM, break deductions. Get results in decimal, HH:MM, and total minutes.
intro: Whether you're a nurse wrapping up an overnight shift, a freelancer billing a client, or an HR manager auditing timesheets, knowing the exact hours between two clock times matters — down to the minute. This free calculator eliminates the mental math and the errors that come with it. Just enter your start time and end time in either 12-hour (AM/PM) or 24-hour format. Have an unpaid lunch break or rest period? Drop those minutes into the break field and they're automatically deducted from your total. Results appear instantly in three formats: decimal hours (ideal for payroll and invoicing), HH:MM (great for schedules and readability), and total minutes (useful for fitness tracking, study logs, and productivity apps). One of the most common headaches in manual time math is the overnight shift — when your end time is earlier than your start time. The calculator detects this automatically and adds the correct 24-hour offset, so a 10:00 PM to 6:00 AM shift correctly returns 8 hours without any workarounds. Break deductions follow FLSA logic: under US federal law, rest breaks of 20 minutes or fewer are generally compensable, while bona fide meal periods (typically 30 minutes or more, with no work duties) may be unpaid. Enter only your unpaid break time in the break field to get your compensable hours. From verifying a contractor's invoice to planning a podcast recording block, this tool gives you a fast, reliable answer you can act on immediately.

explanation:
## What is the time between two times?

Time between two times is the elapsed duration measured in hours and minutes from a start point to an end point. For example, 9:00 AM to 5:30 PM equals 8 hours and 30 minutes. Calculations automatically handle overnight shifts, AM/PM formats, and optional break deductions for accurate work hour tracking.

## How It Works

The calculator converts both times to **minutes since midnight**, computes the raw difference, applies an overnight correction if needed, subtracts break time, then formats the result three ways.

## Formula

```
startMinutes = startHour × 60 + startMin
endMinutes   = endHour   × 60 + endMin

diffMinutes = endMinutes − startMinutes
IF diffMinutes < 0 THEN diffMinutes += 1440   // overnight: add 24 hours

netMinutes   = diffMinutes − breakMinutes
decimalHours = netMinutes ÷ 60

HH = floor(netMinutes ÷ 60)
MM = netMinutes mod 60
```

The constant **1440** is the number of minutes in 24 hours. Adding it when the raw difference is negative correctly handles any shift that crosses midnight without requiring you to enter a date.

## Worked Examples

| Scenario | Start | End | Break | Net minutes | Decimal hours | HH:MM |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standard workday | 9:00 AM | 5:00 PM | 30 min | 450 | 7.50 | 7:30 |
| Half day | 8:00 AM | 12:00 PM | 0 | 240 | 4.00 | 4:00 |
| Overnight shift | 10:00 PM | 6:00 AM | 30 min | 450 | 7.50 | 7:30 |
| Long shift | 7:00 AM | 7:00 PM | 60 min | 660 | 11.00 | 11:00 |

**Overnight example step-by-step:**
- Start = 10:00 PM → 1320 minutes
- End = 6:00 AM → 360 minutes
- Raw diff = 360 − 1320 = −960 → add 1440 → **480 minutes**
- Subtract 30 min break → **450 net minutes**
- 450 ÷ 60 = **7.50 decimal hours** → **7:30**

## Converting Decimal Hours to Pay

Multiply decimal hours by your hourly rate directly: 7.50 hrs × $18.00/hr = **$135.00**. No conversion needed — decimal format is designed for payroll math.

## Limitations

- **Single calendar span only.** The calculator assumes end time is at most 24 hours after start. Shifts longer than 24 hours cannot be computed here.
- **No date logic.** It does not account for Daylight Saving Time transitions. On a DST fall-back night, the actual elapsed time may be 1 hour longer than shown.
- **Break input is manual.** If you have multiple break periods, sum them first, then enter the total.
- **Granularity.** The dropdown uses 15-minute increments. For finer precision, totals are still exact to the minute based on the selected values.

faq.q: How does the overnight shift calculation work?
faq.a: When your end time is earlier than your start time on the clock, the calculator automatically adds 1,440 minutes (24 hours) to the raw difference. Here's the math: a shift starting at 11:00 PM (1,380 minutes from midnight) and ending at 7:00 AM (420 minutes) would give 420 − 1,380 = −960 minutes, which is clearly wrong. Adding 1,440 gives −960 + 1,440 = 480 minutes = 8 hours. This logic handles any overnight scenario up to 23 hours 59 minutes without you having to think about it. Note that this assumes the shift stays within a single 24-hour window — if your shift truly spans more than 24 hours, you'll need a date-aware time tracking tool.

faq.q: What break time should I enter — paid or unpaid?
faq.a: Enter only your unpaid break time in the break field. Under the US Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), short rest breaks of 20 minutes or fewer are generally considered compensable work time and should not be deducted. Bona fide meal periods — typically 30 minutes or more, during which the employee is completely relieved of duties — may be unpaid and should be deducted. So if you take a 30-minute unpaid lunch and two 10-minute paid coffee breaks, enter only 30 minutes. Always confirm break pay rules with your employer or HR department, as some states (California, for example) have stricter break requirements than federal law.

faq.q: What is the difference between decimal hours and HH:MM format?
faq.a: Decimal hours express fractional time as a decimal number — for example, 7 hours and 30 minutes becomes 7.50. This format is essential for payroll math: multiply 7.50 × $20/hr = $150.00 (no conversion needed). HH:MM format expresses the same time as 7:30 and is more intuitive for schedules, clocks, and human readability. The two formats are mathematically equivalent — just different representations. This calculator provides both so you can use whichever fits your context: decimal for invoices and payroll software, HH:MM for schedules, timesheets, and reports.

faq.q: How do I manually convert decimal hours to hours and minutes?
faq.a: Take the decimal portion (everything after the decimal point) and multiply it by 60 to get minutes. Examples: 8.75 hours → 0.75 × 60 = 45 minutes → 8 hours 45 minutes. 6.33 hours → 0.33 × 60 ≈ 20 minutes → 6 hours 20 minutes. 9.17 hours → 0.17 × 60 ≈ 10 minutes → 9 hours 10 minutes. The reverse is also straightforward: divide the minutes portion by 60 and add to the whole hours. 4 hours 45 minutes → 45 ÷ 60 = 0.75 → 4.75 decimal hours. The calculator performs all of this automatically, but the manual method is a useful sanity check.

faq.q: Can I use this calculator for payroll purposes?
faq.a: Yes — the decimal hours output is specifically designed to plug directly into payroll calculations. Multiply decimal hours by the employee's hourly rate to get gross wages for that shift. For example, 8.50 hours × $17.50/hr = $148.75 gross. That said, this tool is best used as a quick verification aid, not a replacement for certified payroll software or official time-tracking systems. It doesn't store records, apply overtime rules (like time-and-a-half after 40 hours per week under FLSA), account for state-specific wage laws, or integrate with tax withholding. For official payroll processing, always reconcile against your time clock records and payroll platform.

faq.q: Does this calculator account for Daylight Saving Time (DST)?
faq.a: No — and this is an important limitation to understand. The calculator performs pure arithmetic on clock times with no date context. On the night clocks spring forward (second Sunday in March in most US states), clocks jump from 2:00 AM to 3:00 AM, making that night's shifts one hour shorter than the clock difference suggests. On the night clocks fall back (first Sunday in November), clocks repeat the 1:00–2:00 AM hour, making shifts one hour longer. If you work these specific transition nights, manually adjust: subtract 1 hour for spring-forward shifts, add 1 hour for fall-back shifts. For all other nights and days of the year, DST has no effect on this calculation.

faq.q: What if my start and end times are exactly the same?
faq.a: The calculator will return 0 hours 0 minutes (0.00). This creates an ambiguity for full 24-hour shifts — there's no way to distinguish a zero-duration entry from a complete 24-hour shift using clock times alone without a date. If you worked a full 24-hour on-call period or a double shift that rounds back to the same time, you have two options: (1) split it into two logical segments and add the results, or (2) use a date-and-time calculator that accepts both a calendar date and a clock time. For standard work shifts (anything under 24 hours), this edge case won't apply.

faq.q: How do I calculate hours for a split shift?
faq.a: Run the calculator once for each segment, then add the decimal results together. Example — a restaurant worker with a split shift: Segment 1: 9:00 AM to 1:30 PM = 4.50 hours. Segment 2: 4:00 PM to 9:30 PM = 5.50 hours. Total: 4.50 + 5.50 = 10.00 hours. If there are unpaid break periods within each segment, enter them during the respective calculation. The unpaid gap between the two segments (1:30 PM to 4:00 PM in this example) is not entered anywhere — it's simply not included in either calculation, so it's automatically excluded from total paid time.

faq.q: What is the maximum shift duration this calculator can handle?
faq.a: The calculator handles up to 23 hours and 59 minutes (1,439 total minutes) of gross time before any break deduction. This comfortably covers the longest single-period shifts found in most industries — including 12-hour hospital shifts, 14-hour trucking on-duty periods, and extended production days. After break deduction, the net result can be anything from 0 minutes up to the gross maximum. If you need to calculate time across a period longer than 24 hours (for example, a 36-hour on-call rotation), you'll need to split the calculation into segments or use a date-time difference tool that accepts full timestamps.

faq.q: Why does the result show 8.00 instead of just 8?
faq.a: The output is always formatted to two decimal places for consistency. When you're working with multiple shift calculations — say, five days of timesheets — having uniform decimal formatting (8.00, 7.75, 6.50, 8.25, 7.00) makes it much easier to add columns in a spreadsheet or compare entries. The two-decimal format also makes it immediately clear that the value is a decimal number ready for multiplication, not an integer that might be confused with a count of something else. Mathematically, 8.00 and 8 are identical — the formatting is purely for clarity and usability.

faq.q: Can I calculate hours for time zones or remote teams across different time zones?
faq.a: This calculator works only on clock times within a single time zone. For scheduling or billing across time zones, you'll need to first convert all times to a common reference (typically UTC or the client's local time) before entering them. For example, if a consultant in New York (ET) starts a call at 9:00 AM ET with a client in Los Angeles (PT, 2 hours behind), that's 7:00 AM PT. The calculator doesn't know about time zones — you just enter the two clock times as you've standardized them and it calculates the difference accurately. For complex international team scheduling, use a dedicated world clock or time zone converter first.

faq.q: How accurate is the total minutes output, and when is it most useful?
faq.a: The total minutes output is mathematically exact — it's the foundation from which both decimal hours and HH:MM are derived. Total minutes is especially useful in contexts where you don't want to deal with fractions or colons: fitness tracking apps (many log workouts in minutes), project management tools that bill in minute increments, academic research logging, or comparing durations quickly (480 minutes vs. 510 minutes is more immediately comparable than 8.00 vs. 8.50 hours for some people). It's also a useful sanity check — if your HH:MM result seems off, confirming the raw minutes makes it easy to spot any input errors.
